covers.quote: Spell out most acronyms on first use
Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.
Write well-known acronyms or initialisms first and follow with the full term in parentheses.
You don’t need to define some acronyms and initialisms on first use.

examples.note: Defines term in full with initialism in parentheses on first mention.

parts.quote: The Department of Social Services (DSS) manages a range of benefits and payments for eligible Australians. DSS helps support communities through a number of programs and services.

examples.note: Well-known acronym first, followed by the full term in parentheses.

parts.quote: All living organisms have DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) within their cells. DNA tells cells what proteins to make.

rules.quote: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention.
rules.specification: Unless an acronym or initialism is widely known or a common lexicalised word, write out the term in full followed by the acronym in parentheses at first mention (or vice versa for widely known acronyms).
rules.violation_condition: an unfamiliar acronym or initialism used without being defined at first mention
when: You don’t need to define some acronyms and initialisms on first use, including some place names (NT, ACT), time of day (am, pm), some organisational names (BHP, Qantas), and terms that began as acronyms but are now words in their own right (radar, scuba, sonar).
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Consolidates the heading and specific rules for defining acronyms on first mention into a single rule with exceptions.

covers.quote: Include a list if content relies on many acronyms and initialisms
You don’t need to include a glossary if:

rules.quote: For content with many specialised acronyms and initialisms, provide a glossary – a list of terms and their meaning that users can refer to.
rules.specification: Provide a glossary when content relies on many specialised shortened forms.
rules.violation_condition: content containing many specialised acronyms and initialisms without a glossary or list of terms and their meanings
when: You don't need to include a glossary if there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms, each one is only in a very limited section of text, and each one is spelt out when first mentioned.
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Combines the guideline on including a glossary with its explicit exceptions.

covers.quote: Don’t end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop
The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

examples.note: No full stop after COAG.

parts.quote: Will you be attending COAG this month?

examples.note: No full stop after B2B.

parts.quote: I’m working on a B2B project at the moment.

examples.note: A full stop after initialism at the end of a sentence.

parts.quote: She’s now working in FOI.

examples.note: No full stop after ASIC when question mark ends sentence.

parts.quote: Is the company being investigated by ASIC?

rules.quote: Don’t place a full stop after the acronym or initialism.
rules.violation_condition: an acronym or initialism followed by a full stop (except when ending a sentence that has no other trailing punctuation mark)
when: The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Heading and paragraph state the rule, followed by its exception.

examples.note: Common noun term spelt out in lower case.

parts.quote: EIS for ‘environmental impact statement’

examples.note: Common noun term spelt out in lower case.

parts.quote: TB for ‘tuberculosis’

rules.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents common nouns, don’t begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: words in the spelt-out form of an acronym or initialism capitalized when they are common nouns rather than proper nouns
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Explicit instruction on capitalisation of expanded forms for common nouns.

examples.note: Proper noun words capitalised.

parts.quote: ASIO [Australian Security Intelligence Organisation]

examples.note: Proper noun words capitalised.

parts.quote: OPC [Office of Parliamentary Counsel]

rules.quote: If the acronym or initialism represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter (excluding words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’).
rules.violation_condition: words in the spelt-out form of a proper noun acronym or initialism (other than minor connecting words like 'of' and 'and') not starting with a capital letter
when: Excludes minor connecting words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Explicit requirement for capitalisation of proper noun expansions.

covers.quote: Avoid plural and possessive forms on the first use

examples.note: Defined in singular form first, pluralised only in subsequent mentions.

parts.quote: It’s compulsory for certain businesses to have an Australian Business Number (ABN). The Australian Business Register manages applications for ABNs.

examples.note: Defined in non-possessive form first, possessive used in subsequent mention.

parts.quote: The University of New South Wales (UNSW) has a new student policy. UNSW’s policy is popular with its staff and students.

rules.quote: Avoid using the plural or possessive of an acronym or initialism when you define it.
rules.violation_condition: an acronym or initialism used in plural or possessive form at the point of definition (e.g. 'ABNs' or 'UNSW's' upon first mention with definition)
rules.why: G-4: Rule prohibiting plural/possessive forms during definition.

covers.quote: Quote acronyms and initialisms the same way as the speaker
When quoting an exact phrase, write exactly what the speaker said. If they used an acronym or initialism, quote it.

examples.note: Full term supplied in square brackets within direct quote.

parts.quote: ‘We’re continuing to manage the number of SES [Senior Executive Service] to ensure the Public Service isn’t top heavy,’ he said.

rules.quote: Show the full term in square brackets if users might not recognise the term or if you haven’t already explained it.
rules.specification: When quoting spoken text verbatim containing an unfamiliar or unexplained acronym/initialism, insert the expansion in square brackets.
rules.violation_condition: a quoted acronym or initialism that may not be recognised and has not been explained, presented without the full term in square brackets
rules.why: G-1, G-4: Rule requiring square-bracket expansion of unfamiliar acronyms inside verbatim quotes.
